cīvis (cīves, C. I. L. 3, 966; 3337 et saep.; ceivis, S. C. Bacch. and Lex Thoria; ceus in Tab. Bant.), is, comm. (abl. usually cive:
civi,; , §§ 32 and 33 Zumpt N. cr.; ; ; ; ; ; ; cf. P.; dub. ) [root ki- of κεῖμαι, to lie, abide; cf. κώμη], a citizen (male or female; opp. pe regrinus,; ; ; opp. advena,; or to hospes,; or to hostis,; ; ).
In gen.
(Very freq. in all periods and kinds of composition.) Vahl.; : optati cives, populares, incolae, accolae, advenae omnes, Date viam, etc.,: quod civis cum civi agat,: cives cum civibus de virtute certabant,—
In fem.: Attica,: civis femina,; ; : civis virgo,; : Romana,; ; : civis Romanus, Enn. ap. P. (Ann. v. 174 Vahl.); ; . —Concerning the political rights of the civis Romanus (opposed to peregrinus or hostis), v. Zimmern, Rechtsgesch. 2, § 123 sq.; Dict. of Antiq. p. 260 sqq.—
Esp., a fellow-citizen (for which, in late Lat., concivis): Lunaï portum cognoscite cives, Enn. ap. (Ann. v. 16 Vahl.); ; .—So particularly, civis meus, tuus, etc., my, thy fellow-citizen, Cato ap. ; ; ; ; ; .—In fem.: defende cives tuas, senex,.—
A subject: imperare corpori, ut rex civibus suis,.—
Figuratively: civis totius mundi,a citizen of the world,.

la:noun:civitas.html:
cīvĭtas, ātis (
gen. plur. civitatium, ; ; ; ; ; ; ; Drak.; 42, 30, 6; 42, 44, 1; 45, 34, 1; ; N. cr.; Oud.; Cornut. ap. P.; cf. ; P.; Neue, Formenl. 1, 268), f.
civis
.
Abstr., the condition or privileges of a (Roman) citizen, citizenship, freedom of the city (upon its conditions, v. Zimmern, Rechtsgesch. 2, § 123 sq.; Dict. of Antiq. p. 260 sqq.): Cato, cum esset Tusculi natus, in populi romani civitatem susceptus est: ita, cum ortu Tusculanus esset, civitate Romanus, etc.,: donare aliquem civitate,; ; ; ; ; ; : dare civitatem alicui,; ; ; ; ; : accipere aliquem in civitatem,

: adsciscere in civitatem,: ascribere aliquem in civitatem,: aliquem foederatis civitatibus ascribere,: in aliis civitatibus ascriptus,: assequi,: consequi,: deponere,: decedere de civitate,: dicare se civitati,: in civitatem,: eripere,: habere,: impertiri civitatem,: furari civitatem,: petere,: Romanam assequi,: adipisci,: Romanam usurpare,; : amittere civitatem,: adimere,; : petere,: negare,: jus civitatis,; : recipere aliquem in civitatem,; ; : relinquere,: retinere civitatem,: retinere aliquem in civitate,: ademptio civitatis,: commemoratio,: nomen,: ereptor,.—

Trop.: ut oratio Romana plane videatur, non civitate donata,; cf.: civitate Romanā donare agricolationem,: verbum hoc a te civitate donatum,naturalized,; ; .—More freq.,
Concr., the citizens united in a community, the body - politic, the state, and as this consists of one city and its territory, or of several cities, it differs from urbs, i.e. the compass of the dwellings of the collected citizens; but sometimes meton., = urbs, v. B.: concilia coetusque hominum jure sociati, quae civitates appellantur,: tum conventicula hominum, quae postea civitates nominatae sunt, tum domicilia conjuncta, quas urbes dicimus, etc.,; cf.: omnis populus, qui est talis coetus multitudinis, qualem exposui; omnis civitas, quae est constitutio populi; omnis res publica, quae populi res est, etc.,: quia sapiens non sum, nec haec urbs nec in eā civitas ... non dubitavisset, quin et Roma urbs (esset), et eam civitas incoleret,: aucta civitate magnitudine urbis,: Orgetorix civitati persuasit, ut de finibus suis cum omnibus copiis exirent, Oud.; so ; 1, 19; 1, 31; cf. Sisenn. ap. : civitates aut nationes devictae,; ; : io triumphe non semel dicemus civitas omnis,; cf. and 18: cum civitas in foro exspectatione erecta staret,; so ; ; ; ; ; ; : civitates aut condere novas aut conservare jam conditas,; ; ; : omnis civitas Helvetia in quattuor pagos divisa est,: quae pars civitatis Helvetiae, etc.,: non longe a Tolosatium finibus, quae civitas est in provinciā,: Ubii, quorum fuit civitas ampla atque florens,: Rhodiorum civitas, magna atque magnifica,; cf. : Heraclea quae est civitas aequissimo jure ac foedere, et saep.: administrare civitatem,: mutari civitatum status,; so, civitatis status,; : (legibus) solutis stare ipsa (civitas) non possit,: lege civitatis,; cf. : mos civitatis,; ; .—Of Plato's ideal republic: si in illā commenticiā Platonis civitate res ageretur,.—
Trop.: civitas caelitum,: ut jam universus hic mundus una civitas sit communis deorum atque hominum existimanda,.—
Meton., = urbs, a city (rare and mostly post-Aug.; not in Cic. or Cæs.): civitatem incendere, Enn. ap. (Trag. 382 Vahl.): cum errarem per totam civitatem,; cf. : Lingonum,; : ab excidio civitatis,; 1, 69: circumjectae civitates,: muri civitatis,; : pererrata nocturnis conversationibus,: expugnare civitatem,; cf.: expugnandae civitates,: plurimas per totum orbem civitates, terrae motu aut incendio afflictas restituit in melius,; cf. ; ; .—
Esp., the city, i. e. Rome and its inhabitants, ; ; .

la:adj:civilis.gloss: civic, civil (of or pertaining to citizens)
senses: civic, civil (of or pertaining to citizens)
public, political (of or pertaining to public or political life)
courteous, polite, civil, affable, urbane
la:adj:civilis.html:
cīvīlis, e, adj.
civis
.
Of or pertaining to citizens, civil, civic (class. in prose and poetry, and very freq.): sanguine civili rem conflant, by the blood of citizens, * ; : conjuratio,: bellum,; : bella,; : genus belli,; ; ; ; : facinus,.—So De Bello Civili, the title of a portion of the Commentaries of Julius Cæsar, : discordia,: dissensio,: discidii specie,: irae,: acies,: arma,civil war,; : aestus,: Mars,: busta,: victoria,; ; : praeda, et saep.: mos consuetudoque,; cf.just before: instituta civilia: conciliatio et societas,: facinus,: clamor,; cf. robur,: curae,: quercus = corona civica (v. civicus, I.),: civilis dies, the civil day (from midnight to midnight; opp. to the naturalis dies, from the rising to the setting of the sun), ; ; : amor (opp. to naturalis),between citizens,.—
Esp.: jus civile.
In gen., private rights, the law, as it protects citizens in their status, property, etc.: jus civile est aequitas constituta iis, qui ejusdem civitatis sunt, ad res suas obtinendas,: sit ergo in jure civili finis hic: legitimae atque usitatae in rebus causisque civium aequabilitatis conservatio,: qui jus civile contemnendum putat, is vincula revellit judiciorum, etc.,; ; ; Gai ; ; opp. jus naturale: quodam tempore homines nondum neque naturali neque civili jure descripto fusi, etc.,.—
The body of Roman law relating to private rights, the Civil Law: ut si quis dicat jus civile id esse, quod in legibus, senatūs consultis, rebus judicatis, juris peritorum auctoritate, edictis magistratuum, more, aequitate consistat,: hoc civile (jus) quod dicimus (opp. causa universi juris ac legum),: de jure civili si quis novi quid instituit,; opp. jus nationum,; opp. jus praetorium, the precedents of decisions by the prætor: nam quod agas mecum ex jure civili ac praetorio non habes,; ; cf. pr. and § 1.—
In narrower sense, the code of procedure, the forms of process in the Roman law: civile jus, repositum in penetralibus pontificum, evulgavit (Licinius), Weissenb. ad loc.: jus civile per multa saecula inter sacra caerimoniasque deorum abditum, Cn. Flavius vulgavit,; cf. sqq.; plur.: inteream si... novi civilia jura,.—
Relating to public or political life, political, public, state-: scientia,politics, political science,; : quaestiones,: officia,, and 2, 4, 27: civilium rerum peritus,: mersor civilibus undis,: vir, a statesman, πολιτικος, Quint. prooem. § 10; 11, 10, 15; 12, 2, 7; 12, 2, 21; 11, 1, 35.—
Esp. civil, opp. military (first in Livy): is gravis annis non militaribus solum sed civilibus quoque abscesserat muneribus,; cf.: civilis res haud magnopere obeuntem bella excitabant,.—
Trop. (cf. popularis, and the Gr. κοινός), demeaning one's self as a citizen; hence of distinguished persons, courteous, polite, civil, affable, urbane (so not before the Aug. per.; esp. freq. in Suet.; in Quint. only once): quid enim civilius illo?: sermo,: animus,; ; ; ; ; cf. ; : parumque id non civile modo sed humanum etiam visum,unbecoming a private citizen,: et humano ingressu, Spald.: incessu,: civile ingenium, mira comitas,; cf. : arma, : civile rebatur, misceri voluptatibus vulgi,; cf. ; 3, 22; ; : civilis circa amicos,: in cunctos,.—Sup., ; .—As subst.: cīvīle, is, n., courtesy: si quicquam in vobis non dico civilis sed humani esset,.—Hence, adv.: cīvīlĭter.
(Acc. to I.) Citizen-like: vivere, Cic. ap. : certare, Cael. ap. ; ; ; ; Gell. praef. § 13.—
In judicial language, civilly (opp. criminally): agere,; ; .—
(Acc. to 2.) As becomes a citizen, courteously, kindly, ; ; ; ; .—Comp.: civilius,; .—Sup.: civilissime,.

senses: courtesy, civility

la:adj:civicus.html:
cīvĭcus, a, um, adj.
civis
.
Of or pertaining to citizens, civil, civic, citizens (more rare than the class. civilis, and, except in the phrase civica corona, mostly poet.): jura,: motus,: rabies,; ; cf. furor,: bella,: invidia,: arma pro trepidis reis,i. e. defence before a tribunal,.—
Esp. corona civica, the civic crown, made of oak leaves (hence, civilis quercus, , and querna corona. ; ), the crown of highest distinction, except the corona obsidionalis, and bestowed upon him who had saved the life of a fellow-citizen in war; its inscription was: OB CIVEM (CIVES) SERVATVM (SERVATOS),; ; ; ; ; Liv 10, 46, 3, Dict. of Antiq. p 310. —Also subst.: cīvĭca, ae, f.: civicam mereri,: aliquem civicā donare,: servati civis decus,—
Of or pertaining to a town or city: errare intra muros civicos, Plaut. Fragm. ap. P. (in Liv. 1, 40, 2, vicinae, not civicae, is the true reading).—No comp. or sup.

senses: politics, the art/practice of government
courteousness, politeness
civility, moderation, restraint
humanity, community, people

cīvīlĭtas, ātis, f.

.
